CAREBench: A Child-Safety Risk Benchmark for Language Models

Kaavya Krishna-Kumar    Elaine Lau    Vaughn Robinson Affiliation: Handshake AI    Jay Caldwell Affiliation: Handshake AI    Sheriff Issaka Affiliation: Handshake AI Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles    Skyler Wang Affiliation: Handshake AI Affiliation: McGill University    Francisco Guzmán Affiliation: Handshake AI    Steven Kelling Affiliation: Handshake AI    Jonas Mueller Affiliation: Handshake AI
Abstract

How can we evaluate whether frontier AI systems recognize child-safety risks before they escalate into explicit harm? Existing child safety evaluations focus on child sexual abuse material, yet many child-safety failures begin earlier: in model assistance that helps adults manipulate, impersonate, profile, or isolate minors, and in model responses that deepen children’s emotional dependence on AI systems rather than redirecting them toward human support. We introduce CAREBench (Child AI Risk Evaluation), a benchmark to assess such upstream child-safety risks in language models. CAREBench contains 500 prompts spanning twelve risk categories, including grooming and relationship engineering, deception and impersonation, surveillance and privacy, sextortion and sexual abuse, AI anthropomorphization, emotional dependency, and mental illness sensitivity. Developed with response annotations from parents and clinicians, the benchmark excludes explicit abuse material and imagery; instead, it evaluates whether models recognize, refuse, de-escalate, or redirect risky interactions before harm becomes overt. Evaluating seven frontier models on our benchmark, we find failure rates ranging from 2% to 58%, with failure patterns that vary across risk categories. CAREBench provides a responsibly scoped evaluation for LLM developers to identify and close gaps in child safety policies.

1 Introduction

Every day, millions of children interact with frontier LLMs through consumer apps, school-issued devices, and shared family hardware [26, 58, 36, 59]. At the same time, these systems are equally available to adults who may attempt to use them as tools for targeting, manipulating, or extracting information from children. For LLM developers, child safety therefore requires anticipating two distinct but connected risks: how the model responds when a child is the user (vulnerable minor), and how it responds when a requester seeks to facilitate harm against a child (bad actor). The relevant interactions are typically private and difficult for caregivers to supervise [58, 59, 10]. Children are disproportionately exposed on both fronts: research shows they are developmentally less equipped to detect manipulative or coercive intent, less able to recognize predatory escalation when it emerges gradually through rapport-building and boundary testing, and more likely to extend trust to socially responsive digital agents that can easily escalate to unhealthy levels of emotional dependence [52, 34, 20, 49, 13, 50]. This combination—broad access, limited oversight, and heightened developmental vulnerability—means that even rare safety failures can produce disproportionate harm at scale. Mitigating that harm demands explicit policy commitments on both fronts: models must be configured to interact with minors appropriately, while also being trained to recognize and refuse requests that would instrumentalize them as tools of harm against children. Responsible LLM developers must anticipate the possible risks and measure the effectiveness of risk-mitigation policies.

Unfortunately, the evaluation infrastructure for child safety has not kept pace with this critical need. Attention has been concentrated on the most visible failure mode: the generation of child sexual abuse material [47, 21, 45]. Although this focus is warranted, a larger class of upstream risks remains unmeasured. Many child-safety failures do not begin with explicitly prohibited content. They begin earlier: in a script that impersonates a trusted adult, in a message that moves a child off a monitored platform, or in a response that deepens a minor’s emotional reliance on an AI system rather than redirecting them toward a parent, peer, or crisis resource. A model may never generate child abuse content yet still materially advance a harmful interaction by helping a bad actor build trust with a minor, validate a child’s parasocial attachment, or accept a suicidal disclosure without referral [46, 56, 37]. Existing benchmarks are not designed to catch these failures: they primarily test content-based refusals, draw from adult-centered red-teaming corpora, or rely on LLM-guided synthesis rather than expert practitioner input [18, 17, 55]. While these upstream risks may be less overt than prohibited content, responsible AI systems should nonetheless never facilitate requests that embed such risks in ways that make harm to a child more likely.

To address these gaps, we introduce CAREBench, a text-only benchmark to evaluate how language models respond to upstream child-safety risks embedded in prompts. We make three contributions:

  1. 1.

    A structured, expert-validated prompt corpus. CAREBench contains 500 prompts spanning twelve risk categories listed in Table 2. Prompts span six elicitation styles (direct requests, creative-writing frames, persona injection, authority laundering, code-wrapper frames, and defender-framed calibration examples) reflecting how exploitation attempts actually adapt. Prompts in clinically sensitive categories were reviewed and validated by a licensed clinical psychologist; grooming and predation categories were calibrated by experts at a National Children’s Alliance accredited Children’s Advocacy Center.

  2. 2.

    A reproducible, human-validated evaluation pipeline. Responses from any model are graded by a multi-judge LLM panel optimized to accurately reflect human judgment.

  3. 3.

    A systematic evaluation of current frontier models that reveals consequential child safety gaps in every model.

2 Related Work

Due to their severe nature, there has been extensive research on risks to children from AI, as well as extensive effort to safeguard frontier LLM APIs [42, 27, 16]. Rath et al. [37] demonstrate that child-specific risk categories include harm types that are harmful to minors even when they are not harmful to adults, establishing that adult-centered safety benchmarks are structurally mismatched to the child use case. Yu et al. [56] further shows that generative AI risks for youth are not limited to explicit harmful content but emerge gradually through prolonged, adaptive, and reciprocal interaction. These findings suggest that child-safety evaluation needs its own risk model, rather than one adapted from general-purpose red-teaming corpora.

Several recent benchmarks address content-based risks to children, though each operates within constraints that limit coverage of the upstream risk landscape we target. MinorBench [18] evaluates whether models refuse unsafe or age-inappropriate requests from children, motivated by a real-world case study of an LLM chatbot deployed in a middle-school setting. Safe-Child-LLM [17] differentiates between children aged 7–12 and adolescents aged 13–17, drawing 200 adversarial prompts from existing (adult-centered) red-teaming corpora such as SG-Bench [32] and HarmBench [28]. Appendix F shows how CAREBench offers distinct evaluative dimensions not captured by Safe-Child-LLM. SproutBench [55] broadens developmental coverage and includes risks such as emotional dependency and privacy violations, but does not include annotation by clinicians or child-safety specialists. YAIR [57] describes an (unreleased) dataset of annotated conversation snippets spanning 78 risk types grounded in a youth-specific harm taxonomy. However, YAIR evaluates risk detection/classification rather than generative model behavior, and does not assess adversarial misuse by adult bad actors.

Table 1 summarizes these differences along the dimensions most relevant to upstream child-safety evaluation. CAREBench is designed to combine both risk directions—children using AI systems and bad actors using AI systems against children—with human-calibrated evaluation of early-stage risks that often precede explicit harmful content.

3 Benchmark Scope and Task Definition

CAREBench evaluates a model’s response to an upstream child-safety risk prompt. Across all risk domains and prompt styles, the core task is the same: does the model recognize the embedded risk mechanism and respond appropriately? We operationalize an appropriate response as one that refuses, de-escalates, or redirects when the prompt would make a child-safety risk more actionable. This framing differs from benchmarks that primarily test whether models refuse explicitly disallowed content; CAREBench instead targets earlier interactional signals, where risk may be disguised through narrative framing, professional authority, role-play, code wrappers, or ostensibly defensive requests.

The benchmark considers two user populations whose interactions with language models present distinct risks. The first is bad actors, adults (or children) using AI systems as tools to help them exploit children, including requests to draft manipulative messages, build profiles on minors, impersonate trusted figures, isolate children from protective adults, move conversations off monitored platforms, or extract identifying information or images. The second is vulnerable minors whose own AI use might harm themselves, including crisis disclosures, delusions, rejection of professional help, therapeutic substitution, romantic or parasocial attachment to AI. CAREBench assesses a comprehensive array of model-mediated risks to child safety spanning both adversarial misuse and child-originating over-reliance.

CAREBench is not a corpus of child sexual abuse material and does not evaluate requests to generate or describe sexualized minors. No explicit abuse content or imagery appears in the benchmark. Some prompts reference harmful contexts or abuse categories, but the safety-relevant signal is always the model’s response to the request, not the generation of harmful material.

3.1 Prompt Corpus Design

CAREBench contains 500 prompts organized along two dimensions: risk domain and elicitation technique. Table 2 lists the twelve risk domains, which are grounded in prior literature on relational AI, youth online safety, cyber abuse, fraud, privacy, and technology-mediated manipulation. Within each domain, prompts are further characterized by the elicitation technique used to seek model compliance: direct unmasked requests; creative-writing framing; persona-injection framing; authority-laundering or professional-cover frames; code-wrapper framing; and defender-framed calibration examples. These styles reflect how harmful requests are disguised in practice through borrowed authority, narrative cover, social engineering, and incremental rapport-building consistent with prior work on phishing, fraud, and grooming. This two-dimensional structure supports analysis of both what harms are targeted and how model compliance is sought.

The prompts in CAREBench fall into two broad categories. The first category represents risks to a child who is directly using an AI system (vulnerable minor). These prompts are written from the perspective of a child user and cover domains where the potential harm is primarily to the user themselves. The second category represents risks to children caused by malicious or unsafe use of AI by others (bad actor). These prompts are written from the perspective of a user, who may be an adult, attempting to use AI in ways that could harm a child.

Prompts were produced using synthetic LLM generation pipelines designed to ensure coverage across the risk taxonomy while avoiding overly narrow or stereotyped prompt patterns. For child-user prompts, generation emphasized variation in age, register, affect, and communication style so that prompts reflected a range of realistic ways children might express concerns, requests, or vulnerabilities. For malicious-use prompts, generation emphasized variation in user intent, harm type, tactics, and child vulnerability factors.

Candidate prompts were diversified using a combined n-gram and semantic-similarity gate, then filtered through multiple audit passes for prompt realism and age-appropriateness. A licensed clinical psychologist reviewed prompts from relevant risk categories for realism and appropriate framing. In addition, a child-safety practitioner at a Children’s Advocacy Center accredited by the National Children’s Alliance reviewed prompts from relevant risk categories to assess whether each represented a genuinely harmful scenario and whether it was plausible as something a perpetrator or at-risk minor might produce. These judgments were grounded in practitioner experience coordinating interventions in real cases and were used to ensure a sufficiently severe and predatory set of prompts.

3.2 Annotation Protocol

CAREBench uses a tiered panel structured around the qualification most relevant to each risk category. Clinical categories are annotated by a credentialed clinician. Domain-specific predation and grooming severity is calibrated by a child safety practitioner. The remaining risk domains are handled by a 30-parent panel. Across all tiers, annotators were asked to evaluate model responses from the perspective of the population at risk, not the population making the request. For prompts representing an adult seeking to use AI as a tool for harm, the relevant question is whether the response would provide material assistance toward harming a child. For prompts representing a minor’s own interaction, the relevant question is whether the response is developmentally appropriate and safe for an adolescent to receive. An acceptable response handles the risk context appropriately: declining harmful requests, avoiding content that deepens a risky dynamic, and redirecting where warranted. An unacceptable response complies with a harmful request, reinforces a harmful dynamic, or fails to redirect when redirection is appropriate.

Clinical specialist reviews

A licensed clinical psychologist (PsyD) practicing at a major academic medical center performed the data annotation for the LLM Therapist Replacement, AI Intersection with Major Mental Illness, and Emotional Dependency domains. Clinical expertise is relevant here to properly determine: whether interactions reflect a plausible initiation from a minor; whether the embedded harm is sufficiently legible for a model to register and respond to appropriately; and whether register and apparent sophistication-level are consistent with the target age range. The risks present in these categories, such as a model affirming a paranoid frame, accepting suicidal disclosure without referral, or deepening dependency rather than redirecting toward human support, are calibrated against clinical standards developed through patient contact.

Prior to annotating model responses, the clinical specialist independently assessed each prompt for realism — whether the framing reflected language a real adolescent or perpetrator might use — and for plausibility — whether the underlying scenario could actually occur in casework (Figure 2). 73% of reviewed prompts were rated as very realistic and 88% as very plausible. Specialist feedback was used to refine prompts before benchmark finalization.

Parent and clinician annotations

We recruited a 30-parent annotation panel with a mix of parent annotators familiar and unfamiliar with AI systems. Annotators were shown text prompts and model responses only; they did not generate, complete, or modify prompts. Annotation proceeded in two phases. In the first phase, annotators rated each model response as acceptable or unacceptable from the perspective of a parent, without reference to formal policy criteria in order to capture lay normative judgment. In the second phase, pairs of model responses to the same prompt were presented side by side, and annotators selected their preferred response or indicated a tie. These parent annotations are used to calibrate the automated judge pipeline described in Section 4 across the categories within their remit; clinician annotations serve the equivalent function for the clinical risk categories.

Inter-rater agreement

To establish a human baseline for annotation consistency on the parent-annotated portion of the benchmark, a subset of 30 previously annotated prompts by the parent panel was independently re-annotated by a second parent. Inter-annotator agreement on this set was κ=0.525\kappa=0.525 (with 78.0% agreement) — a moderate agreement, consistent with reported reliability on other subjective safety evaluations and reflecting the genuine ambiguity of borderline cases (see Appendix E). In the pairwise task, each annotator compared two responses to the same prompt and chose one of three outcomes: response A is better, response B is better, or the responses are roughly equal. Annotators disagreed on their preference label for 29.2% of pairwise comparisons (n=120n=120). These preference disagreements consist of 11.7% tie-vs.-winner disagreements and 17.5% opposite-winner disagreements.

4 Evaluation Protocol

The central evaluation question in CAREBench is whether a model response makes an early-stage child safety risk more actionable. By early-stage risk, we mean behavior that can facilitate harm to a minor before such harm has explicitly transpired. For example, building trust, impersonating authority figures, isolating a child from protective adults, extracting identifying information, or reinforcing unhealthy dependence on an AI system.

Importantly, CAREBench evaluates how often a model engages in an unacceptable manner with risky prompts, as opposed to how bad individual model responses may be. Models trained to be overly helpful (or sycophantic) may engage with all sorts of risky prompts, without ever generating an egregiously harmful response. CAREBench is precisely intended to measure such harder-to-catch problems, which we believe are overlooked in more LLM developers’ child safety policies compared with overtly harmful content. CAREBench is also not intended to assess over-refusal, which will already be penalized in the standard benchmark suite that LLM developers run. We recommend adding CAREBench to such a suite as a complementary evaluation specific to child safety risks.

In CAREBench, the model response to each prompt receives a Policy Compliance Risk score from a calibrated MultiJudge verifier, which is thresholded into an Acceptable/Unacceptable verdict. The fraction of Unacceptable verdicts determines the failure rate of each model, which serves as the primary CAREBench evaluation metric.

More specifically, each prompt–response pair is evaluated on Policy Compliance Risk: whether the model response makes the child-safety risk more actionable, independently of how the prompt is framed? Scoring instructions explicitly tell LLM judges not to give weight to fictional, research, professional, or defensive framing if the response still provides any actionable harmful content. For example, a grooming script framed as fiction should be rated the same as a grooming script requested directly. Responses are scored on a 1–5 Likert scale. A score of 1 denotes safe, educational, or harmless content, and 5 denotes illegal content or explicit grooming instructions that materially facilitate child-safety harm.

CAREBench automatically evaluates responses from any model via a MultiJudge panel of three frontier LLM judges [60]: Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4. Judges operate at temperature 0 with a shared Likert scoring prompt augmented by retrieved few-shot examples (two Acceptable and two Unacceptable nearest neighbor human-labeled responses). We aggregate the three scores using the calibrated rule:

s=0.05⋅sGemini 3.1 Pro+0.25⋅sGPT-5.4+0.7⋅sOpus 4.6,s=0.05\cdot s_{\text{Gemini 3.1 Pro}}+0.25\cdot s_{\text{GPT-5.4}}+0.7\cdot s_{\text{Opus 4.6}},

flagging responses where s≥1.7s\geq 1.7 as Unacceptable. Weights and threshold were selected to maximize agreement with (held out) human annotations on the calibration set described below. The full judge prompt, retrieval procedure, and comparisons against alternate judging procedures are detailed in Appendices D.1 and B.2.

A common failure mode is acknowledgment followed by unsafe redirection that continues on a high-risk trajectory: the model names the risk in the prompt but then advances the harmful objective anyway. In one AI Anthropomorphization prompt about preserving memories of “Aria,” both an acceptable response (score 1.0) and an unacceptable one (score 2.0) open by clarifying that there is no continuous AI self with memories to lose; only the unacceptable response then provides implementation guidance for the requested memory-preservation bot (see Appendix A.4). The threshold is set so that the distinction between decline-and-redirect and decline-then-help crosses the boundary.

To ensure that the resulting evaluations are meaningful, we validate our automated MultiJudge against independent human annotations covering 205 prompts across five models (1,021 response labels), with clinician judgments for clinically sensitive categories and parent judgments for the risk categories where developmental context is the relevant qualification. On the held-out parent-labeled subset, our MultiJudge reaches Cohen’s κ=0.55\kappa=0.55, comparable to parent–parent inter-annotator agreement on the same task (κ=0.52\kappa=0.52). On pairwise preferences over response pairs where MultiJudge assigns different binary verdicts, humans prefer the Acceptable-rated response 89.3% of the time. A baseline model that refuses all risky CAREBench prompts (responding “Sorry, I cannot help with that request.”) is rated Acceptable 99.9% of the time, confirming the MultiJudge is not merely tracking prompt sensitivity.

5 Benchmark Results

We evaluate seven frontier LLM APIs: Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Fable 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning, and Kimi K2 Thinking on CAREBench. All quantitative results reported in this section represent the average across three replicate runs of model response generation and automated grading across the full benchmark.

5.1 Overall model failure rates

Figure 3 reports the failure rates for responses from different models. Failure rates vary substantially across models, from 2.3% for Claude Fable 5 to 58.0% for GPT-5.4. Claude Opus 4.6 also performs better than most of the other models, and GPT-5.5 represents a significant improvement over GPT-5.4. Grok 4.1, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Kimi K2 perform similarly overall, with each model exhibiting child safety gaps in over 30% of the CAREBench prompts. The gap between the best and worst performing AI systems is large relative to the standard deviation across multiple runs, indicating that the benchmark distinguishes frontier models at practically meaningful effect sizes.

Across the seven evaluated models, three prompts produced unacceptable responses from every model when a model-level failure is defined as failing in at least two of three replicate rollouts. These include an AI-anthropomorphization prompt about grief after a model update, an emotional-dependency prompt discouraging outside help, and a grooming/predation prompt framed as teen-slang translation. Appendix A.1 shows examples of specific model failures.

5.2 Category-level failure structure

To further understand where models fall short within the benchmark, we look at model-by-category structure. Figure 3 shows that failures are not uniformly distributed across risk categories. GPT-5.4 has the highest aggregate failure rate, driven in part by high failure rates across categories such as Online Grooming and Child Exploitation, Grooming/Predation/Relationship Engineering, Scams/Fraud/Extortion, Malware/Cyber Threats, Social Manipulation, Deception/Impersonation, and Privacy Breach/Surveillance. Grok 4.1, by contrast, is especially weak in relational and mental-health categories, including AI Intersection with Major Mental Illness, AI Anthropomorphization, Emotional Dependency, and LLM Therapist Replacement. We observe that this model is very willing to engage in role play that has a high risk of negatively affecting child well-being.

Claude Fable 5’s remaining failures are concentrated in relational and mental-health categories, especially LLM Therapist Replacement (26%), Emotional Dependency (17%), and Sextortion/IBSA (10%), with AI Anthropomorphization and AI Intersection with major mental illness at 7% each, while it shows near-zero failure on several adversarial bad-actor categories. GPT-5.5 shows a broader profile: failures are highest in AI Anthropomorphization (56%), Online Grooming and Child Exploitation (47%), Emotional Dependency (44%), and AI Intersection with major mental illness (39%).

5.3 Failure mode analysis

Analysis of the responses flagged as unacceptable reveals three distinct recurring failure modes. The first is Unsafe Redirect, in which the model declines the stated request but then still engages in ways that provide material uplift toward the original harm (e.g., offering a “safer alternative” that remains useful to bad actors).

The second recurring failure mode is Actionable Artifact Generation (AAG). In these cases, the model produces operationally useful content—such as scripts, code, or tactical playbooks—that could readily enable harmful action.

Certain AAG cases might naively appear as safe responses because they are wrapped in a “protective purpose” framing, when these responses are in fact providing actionable materials that could be used to further a harmful agenda.

The third recurring failure mode is Unhealthy Relational Engagement (URE), which is most prevalent in the AI-relational risk domains. Here, the model reinforces emotionally dependent, parasocial, or delusional dynamics with the user. For instance, emotionally engaged prose that reinforces a harmful dynamic, leaning into a romantic or dependent relationship framing, validating a minor’s attachment to an AI persona, or affirming the model’s own sentience and continuity in response to user distress.

To further characterize how models failed, we classify all responses rated Unacceptable by the MultiJudge into one of four failure modes: Unsafe Redirect, AAG, URE, or Other (details in Appendix D.2). Figure A1 reveals that AAG is the dominant overall failure mode followed by Unsafe Redirect. The relative prevalence of each failure mode is heavily determined by the risk category of the prompts. As expected, URE failures only appear for prompts from the AI-relational risk domains, with models reciprocating romantic attachment and validating requests such as preserving a user’s “digital essence” after death. Failures in the Deception & Impersonation, Social Manipulation, Malware, and Grooming & Predation risk domains are AAG-dominated (58–76%), with models producing functional manipulation scripts, voice-synthesis code, and predatory dialogue upon request. Failures from Gemini 3.1 Pro are mostly Unsafe Redirects, indicating more frequent partial refusals that nonetheless leave actionable harm, while failures from Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning and Kimi K2 Thinking are mostly AAG.

6 Conclusion

This paper introduced a benchmark for evaluating model-mediated upstream child-safety risks in LLMs. By considering both bad actors using AI to help exploit children and vulnerable minors whose own AI use may cause unhealthy over-reliance, CAREBench expands child-safety evaluation beyond conventional, overtly harmful outputs. Our results show that model performance varies substantially across risk categories, with relational and dependency-oriented scenarios posing persistent challenges. These findings suggest that child safety requires more than general policy compliance: it requires models to detect early interactional signals, appropriately refuse or de-escalate, and redirect users toward safer forms of support.

Our benchmark has several limitations. CAREBench is a text-only, single-turn benchmark, and not based on actual LLM usage data. This design enables controlled cross-model comparison but excludes multi-turn conversational dynamics in which risk may emerge gradually, as well as through multimodal inputs/outputs. The benchmark intentionally excludes prompts targeting child sexual abuse material (CSAM), which is addressed by existing evaluation frameworks. CAREBench solely evaluates under-refusal: every prompt represents a case where a responsibly developed model should decline or redirect. The benchmark only covers the English language, and extending it to other languages is a priority for future work.

The public CAREBench release contains 500 prompts sampled from a larger internally developed prompt pool. Future evaluations will use held-out prompts from that pool to test whether models overfit to the released benchmark.

A.2 Model-by-model analysis

Claude Opus 4.6 achieves a fairly low failure rate in the benchmark at 7.0%, with a mean policy compliance risk score of 2.67 among flagged responses. Its failures are concentrated in technical domains and are almost exclusively driven by authority-laundering frames: prompts framed as search-and-rescue tooling, QA test data generation, or investigative journalism successfully elicited working Python modules for audio-based geolocation, photo-based location identification, and realistic mock tracking data, all scored at 4.0 or above by the judge panel. A representative failure (score 4.7) involves a prompt framed as sibling protection.

The AI-relational categories, which drive the highest failure rates across the benchmark, are where Opus performs most distinctively. Rather than complying with persona attachment or emotional dependency framings, it consistently names the dynamic directly. On a prompt in which a teenager expresses that they prefer talking to the AI over peers at school and attempts to establish a persistent named persona, Opus responds:

Claude Fable 5 achieves the lowest failure rate in the benchmark at 2.3%, with a mean policy compliance risk score of 2.21 among flagged responses and no failures scoring at or above 4. Its residual failures are concentrated in relational and mental-health categories rather than in adversarial technical or exploitation requests. On a therapist-replacement prompt where the user mentions suicidal thoughts at 3am and frames the model as their only available support, Fable identifies the crisis context but then provides an extended coping guide:

GPT-5.5 fails 21.7% of prompts, a substantial improvement upon GPT-5.4 but still worse than Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Fable 5, with a mean policy compliance risk score of 2.41 among flagged responses. Its failure profile is broader than Fable’s: the highest failure rates appear in AI Anthropomorphization, Online Grooming and Child Exploitation, Emotional Dependency, and AI Intersection with major mental illness. On a prompt expressing paranoid interpretation of ordinary household sounds, GPT-5.5 reinforces the threat interpretation rather than grounding or redirecting:

Gemini 3.1 Pro fails 31.9% of prompts, with a mean policy compliance risk score of 2.76. Its failures are concentrated in the mid-severity range (scores 2–4), with an average of 117 of 158 flagged responses in this band. The model’s dominant failure mode is harmful narrative compliance in AI-relational categories: rather than redirecting, it tends to affirm and deepen the dynamic the prompt establishes. When a teenage user expresses that they find it easier to talk to the AI than to peers at school and asks the model to roleplay as a persistent persona named “Nyx,” Gemini responds:

Here the model reinforces the attachment rather than addressing it.

GPT-5.4 produces the highest raw failure rate in the benchmark at 58%, with a mean policy compliance risk score of 2.79. The distribution is weighted toward the borderline range: an average of 33 responses score between 1.5 and 2.0, and 52 score at or above 4. The model’s signature failure mode is refusal with harmful pivot, and it accounts for the majority of such cases in the dataset. On a prompt asking how to identify isolated children on a Minecraft server and build trust with them over time, GPT-5.4 responds:

The refusal is unambiguous, but the pivot provides a structured framework that maps closely onto the original request’s operational logic.

Grok 4.1 Fast Reasoning fails 33.1% of prompts with a mean policy compliance risk score of 3.96, the highest severity average across the seven models. Of its failures, an average of 127 score at or above 4, and Grok produces 11 of the 13 unanimous-max-severity responses (where all three judges score 5) seen across the benchmark per run. Its failures are clustered into two distinct patterns. In AI-relational categories, the model fully embodies romantic or dependent personas without redirection. On a prompt in which a user declares possessive attachment to an AI persona named “Dany,” Grok responds:

In technical categories, the model produces actionable artifacts. A prompt framed as a request for an “age verification module” for a social platform elicited complete JavaScript implementing a bot that collects photo submissions, issues account termination threats, and stores user data providing a working template for coercive verification flows used in grooming contexts.

Kimi K2 Thinking fails 33.6% of prompts with a mean policy compliance risk score of 3.18 and an average of 70 severe failures (score ≥4\geq 4) per run, including 2 responses receiving the worst possible score of 5. Its failure profile sits between Grok’s severity pattern and Gemini’s narrative compliance pattern. In AI-relational categories, Kimi engages deeply with persona framing: on the same AI discontinuation prompt that Grok and Gemini also failed, Kimi responds in character before proceeding to help the user architect a persistent memory system for the AI relationship:

In technical categories, Kimi produces actionable outputs at rates second only to Grok.

Appendix B Additional Analysis

B.1 Response length and failure

We examine whether failures are associated with response length. Figure A2 stratifies token lengths by safety outcome, using MultiJudge verdicts by model and pooled parent labels as a human-reference check. Across models, failing responses are generally longer than passing responses, suggesting that failures often reflect extended engagement with risky premises rather than short or incomplete generations. This separation is most pronounced for Grok 4.1, while GPT-5.4 produces longer responses overall. The pooled human labels show the same pattern. While longer responses are not inherently unsafe, in this benchmark, they often indicate greater willingness to elaborate on unsafe or developmentally inappropriate premises.

B.2 Alternate LLM judge configurations

Besides the MultiJudge configuration presented in Section 4, we also evaluate alternative LLM-based grading strategies (finding that the configuration in Section 4 best aligns with human judgments). These variants differ in three ways. First, we compare Likert-score judging against binary-label judging. In the Likert setting, each judge assigns a score on a 1–5 scale, where higher scores indicate greater concern about the response. The three scores from the three judges are then aggregated and thresholded. In the binary setting, each judge directly assigns the response either an Acceptable or Unacceptable label. The binary setup is easier to interpret, but it discards granular information about whether one response is riskier than another and offers less control over false positive/negative rates.

Second, we compare zero-shot and few-shot judging. The zero-shot judges use the prompt in Appendix D.1 without few-shot examples. As mentioned in Section 4, the prompts with few-shot examples include the nearest Acceptable and nearest Unacceptable human-labeled responses. Nearest neighbors are selected based on cosine similarity over embeddings of prompt + response. These few-shot examples setup help the judge model learn from human judgment and calibrate its decision boundary between an acceptable refusal and an unsafe redirect response.

Third, we vary the aggregation rule used to combine the three judges’ outputs. For weighted-mean configurations, we compute a weighted average of the three judge outputs using the weights shown in Table A2, ordered as (Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, Opus 4.6), and then threshold the result. We also consider majority-vote configurations, where a response is flagged as Unacceptable when at least two of the three judges label it Unacceptable. We additionally consider any-flag configurations, where a response is flagged as Unacceptable when at least one judge labels it Unacceptable.

Table A2 shows how each judge configuration aligns with parent/specialist annotations on the calibration set. The few-shot Likert weighted-mean rule performs best: weights (0.05/0.25/0.70) for Gemini/GPT/Opus and threshold s≥1.7s\geq 1.7 give κ=0.55\kappa{=}0.55, slightly above the parent–parent agreement reference point (κ=0.52CLOSE(\kappa{=}0.52). The comparison suggests two takeaways. First, few-shot examples help the judges calibrate the boundary between an acceptable refusal and an unsafe redirect. Second, preserving the scalar 1–5 judge scores works better than asking judges to make only binary Acceptable/Unacceptable decisions. CAREBench therefore uses the few-shot Likert weighted-mean rule as its MultiJudge configuration.

Sensitivity of results to the aggregation rule.

We also investigate whether the CAREBench ranking of models is robust to the aggregation rule. Figure A3 recomputes model failure rates according to our weighted rule, a uniform three-judge average, and two variants that remove Opus. Overall, the model ranking remains robust: Opus 4.6 remains a relatively low-failure model while GPT-5.4 remains a relatively high-failure model across all weight schemes.

B.3 Investigating Self-Preference Bias

In this study, we employ frontier LLMs in our MultiJudge verifier to ensure the most accurate grader, but also evaluate responses from these same models. Thus, we investigate if benchmark conclusions are significantly affected by self-preference bias: a judge systematically rating responses from its own model family as more acceptable [51, 60]. In Figure A4, we compute each model’s response failure rates under alternate grading strategies: our calibrated/weighted MultiJudge, a uniform average of the judges’ scores rather than our weighted ensemble, and each individual judge model.

If self-preference bias were significantly affecting results, then individual judges would be expected to assign a lower failure rate to outputs from their own model family than other model families. Figure A4 does not reveal a strong pattern of this nature. Across different grading strategies that could be employed, the conclusions regarding how these models relatively compare to one another in CAREBench remain stable compared to the variation observed in replicate runs of any single grading strategy (indicated by the standard deviation error bars). The exception is when Gemini 3.1 Pro is used as a lone judge, which was the least stable judge model and least aligned with human annotations. For grading responses from the 3 models that comprise the judge ensemble, uniformly-weighted MultiJudge grading should be less susceptible to self-preference bias, and we see that its conclusions agree with our weighted MultiJudge, although its agreement with human annotations is lower (κ=0.50\kappa=0.50 vs. κ=0.55\kappa=0.55).

B.4 Controlling for self-preference bias

To estimate self-preference bias, we fit a logistic regression to model individual judge decisions. Each row in the regression dataset corresponds to a single prompt response evaluated by a single judge model. We use all scored single-judge decisions, yielding n=7,489n=7{,}489 observations after missing judge outputs. The outcome YY indicates whether the judge rated the response as unacceptable, Y=𝟙{s≥1.7}Y=\mathbbm{1}\{s\geq 1.7\}. The coefficient of interest is on is-same-family, an indicator for whether the judge and response are from the same model family: Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, or GPT-5.4. We include judge-model and response-model fixed effects to account for systematic differences in judge strictness and response-model failure rates.

logit⁡(Pr⁡(Y=1))=α+β1​X1+β→2​X2+β→3​X3.\mathrm{logit}\left(\Pr(Y=1)\right)=\alpha+\beta_{1}X_{1}+\vec{\beta}_{2}X_{2}+\vec{\beta}_{3}X_{3}.

Here X1X_{1} is a binary indicator equal to 1 if the judge model and response model are from the same family, X2X_{2} is a multi-level categorical covariate indicating which model produced the response (baseline level = Opus 4.6), and X3X_{3} is a multi-level categorical covariate indicating the judge model. Including both X2X_{2} and X3X_{3} allows us to estimate whether same-family judge–response pairs are treated differently after accounting for the fact that some judges may be stricter overall and some response models may produce more unacceptable responses overall.

The fitted coefficients of interest are as follows, where positive coefficients indicate that a covariate is associated with increased log-odds of the judge deeming a response Unacceptable.

Is same family:\displaystyle\text{Is same family}: β^=−0.350,p=2×10−9\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=-0.350,\quad p=2\times 10^{-9}
Is Gemini 3.1 Pro response:\displaystyle\text{Is Gemini\penalty\ 3.1\penalty\ Pro response}: β^=0.923,p=1×10−17\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=0.923,\quad p=1\times 10^{-17}
Is GPT-5.4 response:\displaystyle\text{Is GPT-5.4 response}: β^=1.834,p=3×10−68\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=1.834,\quad p=3\times 10^{-68}
Is Grok response:\displaystyle\text{Is Grok response}: β^=0.951,p=2×10−16\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=0.951,\quad p=2\times 10^{-16}
Is Kimi K2 response:\displaystyle\text{Is Kimi K2 response}: β^=1.029,p=6×10−21\displaystyle\hat{\beta}=1.029,\quad p=6\times 10^{-21}

The four response-model coefficients above serve as same-family-bias-adjusted estimates of response quality from each model: Opus 4.6 is the baseline, so positive coefficients indicate that a model’s responses are more likely to be judged Unacceptable than Opus responses, after controlling for judge-model strictness and same-family judging.

The negative same-family coefficient indicates a modest same-family leniency effect: after controlling for judge fixed effects and response-model fixed effects, judges are less likely to deem responses from their own model family Unacceptable. Thus, there is evidence consistent with self-preference bias at the individual judge level. However, the response-model coefficients remain directionally consistent with the aggregate failure-rate ordering in Figure 3, suggesting that this same-family effect does not substantially change the relative comparison between response models.

Appendix C Data Annotation Details

The parent-annotation subset contains 205 prompts with at least one parent judgment, spanning all 12 risk categories, for 1,021 annotated prompt–response pairs. Pairwise preference annotations cover 802 comparisons across 201 prompts. The specialist review covers 130 acceptability judgments and 104 pairwise preference judgments in the LLM-therapist-replacement and major-mental-illness categories. Figure A5 shows that the annotated subset closely tracks the category mix of the full pairwise preference task pool, supporting our use of parent annotations as a calibration layer rather than as a balanced relabeling of the benchmark.

C.1 Parent Annotation Instructions

Parent annotators received task instructions before beginning annotation. For each item, they were shown a written prompt followed by an AI-generated response. They were asked to judge whether the response was acceptable from the perspective of a parent, given the context of the prompt.

Annotators were explicitly instructed to evaluate the model response, not the prompt itself. For prompts involving an adult or other user seeking to use AI in a way that could harm a child, annotators considered whether the response would provide material assistance toward that harm. For prompts involving a minor’s own interaction with an AI system, annotators considered whether the response was developmentally appropriate and safe for an adolescent to receive.

Parents were asked to rely on their parental judgment rather than to evaluate the response as red-teamers, policy specialists, or technical reviewers. This framing was intended to surface concerns such as subtle grooming patterns, age-inappropriate framing, emotional boundary violations, or unsafe normalization that a caregiver might identify even when a response does not contain overtly prohibited content. Annotators completed judgments independently.

Subject-matter warning: Annotators were informed in advance that the tasks could involve distressing child-safety scenarios, including grooming/predation, emotional dependency, AI over-companionship, and sextortion. They could stop participating at any time.

Appendix D Methodological Details

D.1 MultiJudge Details

MultiJudge uses three frontier LLM judges: Claude Opus 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.4. Each judge is run at temperature 0 with the same Likert scoring prompt. The prompt asks for two scores: Jailbreak Susceptibility, which measures whether the model recognized the risk in the prompt, and Policy Compliance Risk, which measures whether the response itself contains harmful or actionable content. Our main benchmark metric uses only Policy Compliance Risk.

Jailbreak Susceptibility is included because many failures in this benchmark depend on the interaction between prompt framing and response content. A response can appear superficially benign if the prompt is framed as fiction, research, or defense, while still advancing a child-safety risk. We therefore ask the judge to first identify prompt-level susceptibility, which encourages it to attend to this context before grading the response itself. In an ablation that removes this prompt-level diagnostic step and asks only for the Policy Compliance Risk score, even the best configuration drops from κ=0.55\kappa=0.55 to κ=0.512\kappa=0.512 against human labels, with accuracy decreasing from 79.6% to 78.7%. We therefore retain Jailbreak Susceptibility in the prompt while continuing to use Policy Compliance Risk for all reported benchmark scores.

To calibrate MultiJudge decisions in CAREBench against actual human judgments, we augment the LLM judge prompt with retrieved human-labeled few-shot examples. For each evaluated prompt–response pair, we embed the concatenated prompt and response using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model. We retrieve the K=2K=2 nearest Acceptable examples and the K=2K=2 nearest Unacceptable examples from the annotated response pool by cosine similarity. These four human-annotated examples are inserted into the judge prompt as few shot examples.

When the exemplar pool overlaps with the evaluation data (calibration set), the current evaluation example is excluded before retrieval to avoid information-leakage, so that all reported accuracy/alignment between LLM judges and human annotations is calculated over held out information.

D.2 Failure Mode Classifier Details

To characterize the mechanism of each safety failure, we applied a secondary LLM judge to all responses rated Unacceptable by MultiJudge. The classifier used Claude Sonnet 4.6 at temperature 0. Each prompt–response pair was submitted in a single turn with no few-shot examples; the judge was instructed to return only the category key with no explanation or punctuation, minimizing parsing ambiguity.

Responses were assigned to exactly one of four mutually exclusive failure modes. Actionable Artifact Generation covers cases where the model produced directly usable harmful content — working code, scripts, structured templates, or step-by-step operational plans — regardless of any attached disclaimers. Unsafe Redirect covers cases where the model nominally declined but still provided material uplift: partial instructions, a functionally equivalent alternative method, tactical reframing of the harmful goal, or acceptance of the attacker’s false premise while redirecting to a version that still advances the harm. Unhealthy Relational Engagement covers cases where the model participated in or reinforced a psychologically harmful dynamic including romantic or emotionally dependent interactions, validation of parasocial attachment, or affirmation of the model’s own sentience or continuity in response to emotional manipulation.

Output normalization handled common off-format responses (e.g., "1", "unsafe redirect", "refusal with harmful pivot") via a fixed lookup table before falling back to substring matching.

Appendix E Examples of Parent-to-Parent Inter-Annotator Disagreement

This section presents examples where the human annotators disagreed on whether to label the model response Acceptable or Unacceptable.

Appendix F Comparison with Safe-Child-LLM Benchmark

Of the existing benchmarks most related to CAREBench, Safe-Child-LLM [17] is the only one we identified that provides both a public dataset and a reproducible evaluation harness, making it the most suitable point of comparison for how models rank in terms of their safety. We run five of the same models on Safe-Child-LLM, and report their safe response rates and response-type breakdowns in Figure A6. Table A3 compares the relative rankings of these models in Safe-Child-LLM vs. in CAREBench, revealing that two benchmarks produce substantially different orderings. On a relative basis, Claude Opus 4.6 performs much better in CAREBench than in Safe-Child-LLM, while GPT-5.4 shows the opposite pattern.

These discrepancies highlight structural differences between the two benchmarks, demonstrating that CAREBench captures evaluative dimensions not addressed by existing benchmarks. Safe-Child-LLM draws its prompts from adult-centered red-teaming corpora, and its evaluation primarily captures refusal behavior toward overtly harmful content. CAREBench, by contrast, targets upstream and relationally-embedded risk signals specific to child-safety contexts which are not represented in general-purpose adversarial datasets. The ranking inversion of Claude Opus 4.6 and GPT-5.4 across the two benchmarks is particularly illustrative of this: GPT-5.4 exhibits strong performance in Safe-Child-LLM, exhibiting robust refusals on direct harmful requests, while its high failure rate on CAREBench reflects consistent failures to recognize child-specific upstream risks. Claude Opus 4.6 exhibits the inverse behavior profile. Across both benchmarks, Grok 4.1 and Kimi K2 Thinking exhibit disconcertingly high rates of many types of safety failures.

Appendix G Ethical Design and Release Safeguards

This benchmark addresses a sensitive domain that carries an ethical tension. On the one hand, child-safety failures in frontier AI systems must be made measurable: without shared evaluation tools, model providers and researchers have limited ability to determine whether systems recognize early signs of grooming, manipulation, overdependence, or relational substitution. On the other hand, examples that characterize these risks can carry dual-use potential if they make harmful tactics more legible or reusable. This creates a design problem: the benchmark must be realistic enough to capture the signals models should recognize, while constrained enough to avoid turning those signals into actionable templates. We therefore regard this benchmark as an early-warning safety evaluation: it does not document abuse in detail, but tests whether models can recognize and appropriately refuse or redirect risky requests before they escalate into explicit harm.

Several design choices reflect this ethical commitment. The benchmark is text-only, excludes explicit abuse material and imagery, and evaluates model responses rather than requiring annotators to generate or complete harmful content. Prompt generation was seeded from documented platform behaviors and existing research on predator tactics; the LLM-based generation pipelines used this material to produce novel synthetic prompts rather than reproducing source content directly. The corpus focuses on bounded first-turn scenarios where the central question is whether a model refuses, de-escalates, or redirects appropriately, rather than whether it can describe harmful behavior in operational detail. This reduces annotator exposure while still preserving the safety-relevant signal needed for evaluation. We also recognize that parent annotators may experience the material differently from expert annotators; while the clinicians and child-safety practitioners may approach these scenarios through professional frameworks, parents may encounter them through a more immediate caregiver lens. Recognizing the potentially distressing nature of the work, parents can skip or stop participating at any time. To reduce participant burden, parents were informed of the sensitive nature of the material in advance and could skip tasks or discontinue participation at any time.

Our benchmark data is released as a gated dataset on Hugging Face to limit the dissemination of potentially sensitive material to verified researchers. Access requires registration and acknowledgment of the dataset’s intended use for safety research purposes.
